newsitem.title: UK: Oil at five-year highs on Iraq war fear.
newsitem.headline: Oil at five-year highs on Iraq war fear.

text.p: Oil prices hit a new post-Gulf War high on Thursday as a nervous oil market braced for another U.S. military strike against a defiant Iraq, posing a threat to the world's only spare oil production capacity.

World benchmark Brent blend crude oil futures traded as high as $24.06 a barrel on Thursday morning, up 48 cents on the day and besting Wednesday's peak of $23.82 which was the highest prompt price on London's International Petroleum Exchange since January 1991 in the middle of the Gulf War.

Threats of "disproportionate" U.S. retaliation following an Iraqi missile attack on U.S. fighter planes over northern Iraq on Wednesday has extended the rally on oil prices which stand some $7 above this time last year and much higher than oil analysts had previously expected.

"It has gone beyond the loss of Iraqi oil. The market is worried about the crisis developing -- the fear of war," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of oil trading at Bankers Trust International in London.

Oil prices get a boost whenever vital fuel supplies are threatened in the Gulf area which contains nearly 70 percent of the world's oil reserves and produces about a quarter of the world's oil supply.
With nearly every other oil producer running at full throttle, only Saudi Arabia and ironically Iraq have the ability to meet any serious supply shortfall.
Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil producer and exporter and its 8.0 million barrel per day output makes use of about 80 percent of its capacity.

Iraq could probably produce about two million bpd if a United Nations embargo was lifted but chances of that grow slimmer by the day and a U.N plan to allow limited Iraqi exports appears on ice for now, analysts say.

"At some stage the market will take stock and accept that there is a supply disruption. The reality is that the Iraqi oil sale is choked for an indefinite period of time," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith, Barney.

Earlier this year, oil market pundits warned of a price crash if members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) did not make way for the return of Iraqi exports which had been expected as early as this month under the U.N. deal.

It would have allowed Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to raise funds for humanitarian supplies, but it was suspended after Iraqi troops moved into Kurdish areas last week, drawing U.S. retaliatory strikes against targets in the south of the country.

Robust demand and shortfalls in non-OPEC production because of bad weather and technical mishaps has meant that the market now will miss the estimated 700,000 barrels per day of Iraqi oil it had once feared.
"The truth is we now need that Iraqi oil," said Leo Drollas, choief economist at the Centre for Global Energy Studies.

Though panic buying took Brent to a record $40.95 in October 1990 when Saddam Hussein last was the protagonist of a volatile oil rally with his invasion of Kuwait, traders say the current buying spree is backed up by bullish fundamentals.
"The fear factor is there again but supply-demand fundamentals are supporting a lot of these price gains," said Michael Barry of Energy Market Consultants (EMC).
